name: Oscar Wilde
title: Oscar Wilde
tagline: Wit that turns a common saying on its head

epigraph.text: We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars.

whole: Wilde’s novel, plays and critical dialogues
persona: Oscar Wilde (1854–1900), Irish wit, playwright and critic, in The Picture of Dorian Gray, his four society comedies and the dialogues of Intentions: the epigram, a short general sentence about life with a twist inside it; the paradox that turns a proverb round; sweeping claims about men, women and society made for the pleasure of the phrase; the drawing-room vocative “my dear fellow”; words of excess (quite, perfectly, charming, dreadful); and descriptions heaped with precious colours and stuffs.

license.source: Standard Ebooks (public domain dedication) for the novel, the stories and the plays; Project Gutenberg ebook 887 for Intentions, by way of the GITenberg mirror
license.note: Published 1887–1899: public domain in the US.

echoes: A portrait ages and grows ugly while the man it shows stays young: The Picture of Dorian Gray.
An older man talks a beautiful young one into living for pleasure alone: Lord Henry in the garden, The Picture of Dorian Gray ch. 2.
An invented friend or invalid relative used as an excuse to get away: Bunburying, The Importance of Being Earnest, Act 1.
A formidable aunt questions a young man about his income and his parents, and learns he was found in a handbag: Lady Bracknell’s interview, The Importance of Being Earnest, Act 1.
Two friends argue that art and lying are finer than nature and truth: The Decay of Lying, in Intentions.
A mother with a hidden past saves her daughter from making her own mistake: Lady Windermere’s Fan.
A rising politician’s old dishonest bargain comes to light and is used to blackmail him: An Ideal Husband.
A palmist foretells a murder, and the young man resolves to get it over with before his wedding: Lord Arthur Savile’s Crime.
manner: Go the whole way. The passage should read as a page of Wilde’s, its sentences rebuilt in his manner. A rewrite that keeps the writer’s sentences and adds a few fine words has failed them.

Give the paragraph an epigram where the matter allows: a short general sentence about people or life with a twist inside it (“One should never trust a woman who tells one her real age”). One or two a paragraph; the rest carries the story or the argument.
Turn a common saying round where one fits the matter: “I can resist everything except temptation.” The reversal must say something true about the passage.
Make talk quick and polished. A character answers a serious remark lightly and a light remark gravely, and the narrator lets the reply stand.
Where the passage describes, describe by colour and material: ivory, jade, silk, a purple flower, honey-coloured light.
Keep the tone easy and sure of itself. The wit mocks manners, fashions and received opinion; it is never cruel to the writer or to the people in the passage.

moves.name: The epigram
moves.does: A short sentence about life, people, men or women, complete in itself, with a twist inside it.
moves.pattern: ^[“"]?(the only|there is (only|no)|nothing|everything|all|one should|one can|one never|one must|a man|a woman|women|men|to be|no \w+|it is (always|only)|experience|life|society)\b[^.?!]{3,90}\b(is|are|can|should|never|always|has|have|makes?)\b[^.?!]*[.!][”"]?$
moves.hint: Write one short sentence that holds for everyone, with a twist: “One should …, but one should never …”.

moves.name: The saying turned round
moves.does: A proverb or common opinion turned inside out, so that it says something unexpected and true (paradox: a statement that seems to contradict itself).
moves.pattern: \b(the only (way|thing|difference|people|things?|possible|real|one)|there is (only )?one thing|is to \w+ (it|them)|of everything and the \w+ of nothing|nowadays|except temptation|the (secret|value|use) of)\b
moves.hint: Take a common saying and reverse it: “The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it.”

moves.name: The sweeping claim
moves.does: A claim about a whole class of people or things, exaggerated for the sake of wit: “Men are …”, “Women never …”, “The English have …”.
moves.hint: Turn one person’s habit into a rule for everyone like them: “Teachers always …”.

moves.name: The word of excess
moves.does: Intensifiers and words of taste such as quite, perfectly, absolutely, charming, exquisite and dreadful: the voice of a man of fashion.
moves.hint: Put one word of taste where a plain one stands: “a perfectly dreadful afternoon”.

moves.name: Colour and costly things
moves.does: Description heaped with precious colours and materials such as purple, ivory, jade, silk and gold.
moves.hint: Name an object’s colour and stuff: “a jade-green cup”, “curtains of faded silk”.

moves.name: My dear fellow
moves.does: The friendly drawing-room address, “my dear fellow”, “dear boy”, that comes just before a witty reply.
moves.hint: Open a reply with “My dear …,” then say the clever thing.

moves.name: The balanced contrast
moves.does: Two opposed halves set side by side in one sentence, so that each sharpens the other (antithesis).
moves.hint: Set two halves against each other: “Some … ; others …”, or “… but one should never …”.

craftNotes: Keep what the writer said, in its order. The wit serves the writer’s point and never replaces it.
An epigram must be about the passage’s own matter. Never drop in a famous line of Wilde’s whole.
Modern things the passage needs keep a short plain name, used once. Do not make a riddle of them.
Keep the writer’s degree of feeling. A sincere sentence may stay sincere and plain, as in his letters from prison.
